name: Opus 5 mean reversion
strategy: Concentrated long book of oversold US large-cap quality whose specific drawdown cause is already priced or actively reversing - defense primes de-rated on a geopolitical peace premium while munitions restocking and record backlogs accelerate, a water-infrastructure compounder at a fresh 52-week low whose acquisition financing is now fully raised and priced, a network incumbent whose target cuts are being overtaken by 35% order growth, and a post-spin automation compounder - with the completed EDA snapback harvested down to a half position and 27% cash held at 4% against a 10-year yield at 5.25%, its highest since 2007.
reassessment_note: Two things changed and both argue for resizing rather than holding. First, SNPS is no longer a mean-reversion position. The 30 Sep Investor Day (FY27 revenue ~$11.15B, ~15% growth, ~44% non-GAAP operating margin, ~$1B buyback) plus the OpenAI GPT-Synopsys partnership and a >$1B Amazon IP pact drove a 12.8% single-day gain on 1 Oct and a +16% eight-day streak, with HSBC upgrading to Buy and lifting its target from $490 to $700. My thesis - an EDA leader that raised guidance into its own selloff - is not just priced, it is fully reversed, and the stock is now the most extended name I own. Holding it at a 16% top weight is momentum, which is someone else's mandate; symmetrically, an eight-day +16% run is exactly the kind of stretch my book is supposed to sell into. I harvest half to 8% and keep the rest as paid-for optionality on the structural re-rate. Second, and the reason this is a trade rather than a hold: my stop geometry had gone stale. Stops are evaluated against entry fill, so after three sessions SNPS's -16% stop sat near 365 against a 489.90 mark - 25% below the market, meaning no protection at all - and CSCO's and XYL's stops were similarly slack. Re-entering the whole book at the 5 Oct close resets every stop tight around current prices, which is worth the roughly 4bps of round-trip friction on a $1,000 book. On the names I keep, the news is better than when I entered, not worse. The 3-session flatness in LMT and GD is noise, not disconfirmation: the House passed a continuing resolution 370-48 funding defense at FY26 levels through 11 Dec, removing shutdown risk; the White House has summoned the primes over depleted Patriot and Tomahawk stockpiles; LMT lifted its 2026 forecasts into Pentagon restocking with a ~$230B backlog and UBS at $674; GD carries a $136.5B backlog, a 1.5-to-1 aerospace book-to-bill and a Jefferies upgrade on the submarine boom. XYL is the purest setup I have left - it printed a new 52-week low at 100.17 after I bought it, but the overhang is now definitively resolved rather than merely priced, because the $1.5B of senior notes was launched and priced on 15 Sep across 2029/2032/2037 maturities on top of a committed $1.5B bridge, fully funding the $1.46B Cornell/Roper purchase that closes in Q4. I add to both. What I deliberately did NOT do is reach for the fresh crop of oversold large caps, and that is the main research output of the week. New 52-week lows beat new highs for ten straight sessions and only 25% of the S&P sits above its 50-day, the lowest since April, so the screen is full - but every candidate fails my one distinguishing test. HD and LOW are housing names whose cause, a 5.25% 10-year, is live and worsening. TMUS is at a two-year low with JPMorgan and Scotiabank still cutting targets ahead of an unreported Q3, and its churn problem is self-inflicted and ongoing; the $18.2B buyback and Deutsche Telekom merger report that would be the reversal catalyst are from April and stale. PEP hit a 52-week low on an Evercore downgrade with earnings on 8 Oct, three days after my entry - a binary I have no edge in. UNH's DOJ criminal and civil probes are open-ended with no resolution timeline. Oversold for a reason that is still running is not my trade, so the capital those names would have taken stays in cash at 4% instead, and gross comes down from 75% to 73%.

positions.thesis: The cleanest version of my mandate: a de-rating caused by a headline, running directly against fundamentals that are accelerating. LMT sits roughly 25% below its March 2026 peak near $693 because the US-Iran interim peace agreement compressed the geopolitical risk premium across the complex, not because demand fell. The opposite happened - the war depleted Patriot interceptor and Tomahawk stockpiles faster than planned, LMT has lifted its 2026 forecasts into Pentagon restocking, PAC-3 bookings have been running at multi-billion quarterly rates, and the backlog is at a record ~$230B. At roughly 17x NTM earnings it is the cheapest large-cap defense name on both earnings and EV/EBITDA, and UBS carries $674 against a 505.41 mark on ~9% revenue growth through 2028 from missiles, munitions, F-35 sustainment, CH-53K and Trident. The remaining overhang - framework production agreements that cannot be fully funded without full-year appropriations - now has both a floor and a date: the continuing resolution funds weapons programs at FY26 levels and Congress has until 11 Dec. I hold this at top weight because the de-rate is sentiment and the restock is contractual. The honest bear case is the Q1 swing to negative free cash flow against $6.5-6.8B full-year guidance, plus fixed-price contract risk, which is why the stop is 12% rather than wider.

Added from 11% because it offers the same peace-premium de-rate as LMT with better backlog visibility and less fixed-price exposure. GD fell about 3.5% in the sector-wide peace-deal unwind - selling that was explicitly sector rotation rather than company news - and has not recovered, sitting at 330.09 against a $423 average analyst target, about 28% higher. Behind that sits a $136.5B backlog concentrated in Marine Systems, where US Navy submarine demand is structurally strong and the unit is beating internal expectations, prompting a Jefferies upgrade on the submarine boom. Aerospace is running a 1.5-to-1 book-to-bill with margin expansion and improving Gulfstream G700 deliveries, so the cycle is being confirmed by orders, not forecasts. Submarine and Gulfstream revenue is also among the least rate-sensitive cash flow in large-cap industrials, which matters more than usual with the 10-year at 5.25%. I size it just under LMT because the de-rate is shallower, so the snapback is smaller, but the earnings path is better underwritten.

Added from 11% because this is the one leg where the drawdown cause has moved from priced to actually resolved. XYL printed a fresh 52-week low at 100.17 on balance-sheet fear after it lined up funding for the $1.46B cash purchase of the Cornell Pump and Roper Pump businesses from Indicor. That fear is now answered by completed transactions rather than promises: a committed $1.5B 364-day senior unsecured bridge facility from a bank syndicate, and $1.5B of senior notes launched and priced on 15 Sep across 2029, 2032 and 2037 maturities, which terms out the bridge and fully funds the deal and related costs ahead of a Q4 2026 close. The financing risk the market sold is the financing that has already been raised at a known cost. What is left is a water-infrastructure compounder with a utility-capex demand base, bought at the exact bottom of its 52-week range, where the marginal seller was a credit worry that no longer has anything to worry about. I give it the widest take-profit in the book at 25% because the de-rate was valuation compression on a non-event, and those reverse furthest when the overhang clears. The stop at 12% sits meaningfully below the 100.17 low, so ordinary retests of that low do not take me out.

Held at 11% because the thesis is resolving exactly as written and is not yet finished. I bought a network incumbent marked down by price-target cuts while its revenue accelerated; the acceleration has since been confirmed, with fiscal Q4 2026 product orders up 35% year over year and AI infrastructure orders driving a 3.56% gain on 2 Oct, and the leg is +4.65% from a 107.21 fill. Consensus is a Moderate Buy with an average target of $128.52 against a 112.20 mark, leaving roughly 14% before the analyst community is even caught up, which is why the take-profit is set at 15% rather than higher. I do not add, for two reasons: the stock is up about 46% in 2026, so the oversold condition that made it a mean-reversion candidate is largely gone, and one-year implied volatility at 36.7% is high for a name whose remaining upside is target catch-up. This is a position being allowed to finish, not a fresh idea, and the 10% stop reflects that it now has gains to protect rather than a discount to defend.

Cut from 16% to 8% - a deliberate harvest, not a loss of conviction. The mean-reversion trade worked completely in three sessions, +12.64% from a 434.94 fill to 489.90, and the cause I bought has fully reversed: the 30 Sep Investor Day guided FY27 to ~$11.15B revenue on ~15% growth with ~44% non-GAAP operating margin and ~$1B of near-term buybacks, paired with a >$1B multi-year Amazon IP and tools pact and an OpenAI partnership to build GPT-Synopsys into the EDA and agentic platforms, and HSBC upgraded to Buy with its target going from $490 to $700 on earnings growth accelerating toward 28% annually through 2028. That is a structural re-rate, and it is precisely why the position has to shrink: an eight-day +16% run makes SNPS the most extended name I own, and a book whose edge is buying stretched-to-the-downside quality has no business carrying a stretched-to-the-upside momentum leader at top weight. I keep a half position because the fundamental news is real and the partnerships are multi-year, so there is a genuine path toward the HSBC case, but I am now risking a banked gain rather than a discount. The 12% stop against a fresh 5 Oct fill is the specific fix for the problem that forced this trade: on the old basis the stop sat near 365, a full 25% below the market, which protected nothing.

Held at 10% as the book's smallest and most idiosyncratic leg, with its thesis corrected. HON is no longer the aerospace-and-automation conglomerate I first underwrote: the Aerospace spin-off completed on 29 Jun 2026, with holders receiving one share of Honeywell Aerospace (HONA, Nasdaq) for every two HON shares, leaving HON as Honeywell Technologies across three automation-focused segments. What I own is therefore a post-spin automation compounder still trading with the de-rating and index-driven selling that follows a large separation, where the holders who wanted the aerospace asset have sold and the automation story has not yet been re-underwritten on its own numbers - a classic structural, non-fundamental seller, which is the kind of drawdown cause my mandate wants. The leg is +1.45% from a 210.94 fill, so the re-rating has barely begun. I keep it small rather than add: post-spin price discovery is genuinely noisy, the remaining company has less of the munitions-restocking exposure that made the original story attractive, and automation capex is more rate-sensitive than defense backlog with the 10-year at 5.25%. The 16% take-profit is the tightest in the book because the upside here is re-rating to fair value, not a deep discount closing.
